title: Impurity-Free Nasicon Solid Electrolytes for High-Performance All-Solid-State Sodium Metal Battery
abstract:
<jats:p>The rapidly growing demand for energy storage systems—driven by the proliferation of electric vehicles, renewable energy integration, and portable electronics—has underscored the resource and cost limitations of lithium-based batteries [1]. As a promising alternative, sodium-ion batteries offer advantages such as the high natural abundance of sodium (2.36% vs. 0.002% for lithium) and lower material cost [2]. Furthermore, all-solid-state sodium metal batteries (ASSSMBs) provide enhanced safety, a higher theoretical capacity (1,166 mAh·g⁻¹), and a lower redox potential (−2.71 V vs. SHE), making them strong candidates for next-generation energy storage systems [3].</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Among the available solid electrolytes for ASSSMBs, Na3Zr2Si2PO12 (NASICON) has emerged as a leading material due to its high ionic conductivity (10⁻3–10⁻4 S·cm⁻1), excellent thermal stability, and wide electrochemical window (~5 V vs. Na⁺/Na). Its robust three-dimensional framework—comprising corner-sharing ZrO₆ octahedra and SiO₄/PO₄ tetrahedra—facilitates efficient Na⁺ transport [4]. Despite these advantages, the conventional solid-state reaction (SSR) synthesis of single-phase NASICON remains challenging due to sodium and phosphorus volatilization at elevated temperatures, which results in the formation of ZrO2 and Na3PO4 impurities [5, 6]. These impurities reduce ionic conductivity and impair interfacial stability with sodium metal [7]. Although alternative synthesis methods such as sol–gel and solution-assisted SSR can suppress impurity formation, they are generally less scalable and more costly [8].</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>In this study, we report the successful synthesis of impurity-free NASICON powders via an optimized SSR method. Phase purity was confirmed by X-ray diffraction (XRD). Densely sintered pellets (>98% relative density) were fabricated without sintering aids. Electrochemical characterization revealed high room-temperature ionic conductivity and low activation energy. Furthermore, the dense microstructure effectively suppressed sodium dendrite formation during cycling, underscoring the material’s suitability for safe and high-performance ASSSMBs [9].</jats:p>
